Keywords: Whatever, Attracts, And

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendering of the poem, with modernized diction and refined phrasing while preserving its original imagery, meaning, and structure:

---

Whatever it may be whose beauty here below
Draws thee to stream and flow,
To wind and curl, to wink and smile,
Shifting thy gait and wile;

Though thy close commerce nothing doth debar
My present quest—for eagles heed not stars—
And still the lesser, by the best
And highest good, is blessed;

Yet, seeing all things that subsist and be
Receive their charge from divinity,
And teach us duty, I shall see
What man may learn from thee.

First, I am sure the subject so esteemed
Is well disposed, for bodies once infected,
Depraved, or dead, can hold with thee
No bond, nor sympathy.

Next, there dwells in it a restless, pure desire,
A longing for thy bright and vital fire—
A desire that never shall be quenched,
Nor can be twisted or wrenched.

These are the magnets that so strongly move,
And labor through the night for thy light and love,
As beauteous shapes, we know not why,
Command and guide the eye.

For where desire—celestial, pure desire—
Has taken root, and grows, and does not tire,
There God a sacred commerce grants,
And sheds his secret on their hearts.

This is the heart he craves; and whosoever will
Freely surrender it, withholding nothing still,
Shall feel that God is ever true—
As hidden herbs put on their green anew.

---

This version retains every idea, image, and argument of the original—the address to a radiant, elusive beauty; the meditation on divine purpose in all created things; the contrast between corrupted and pure desire; and the closing assurance of God’s faithfulness to those who surrender their hearts—while smoothing the syntax and modernizing archaic forms for greater clarity and eloquence.

# Reflections on Divine Purpose and the Soul's Ascent

Below me, I perceive something of remarkable beauty—a fluid, ever-shifting presence that curls and transforms itself through countless guises, moving with a grace that might well captivate a lesser mind. Yet I find myself unconcerned with the intricate mechanics of its inner workings, the how and why of its constant metamorphosis. This is not because such things lack wonder, but because my gaze is fixed upon loftier concerns. Like an eagle soaring through the heavens, indifferent to the stars that glitter so far above its reach, I too look past what merely dazzles the eye in favor of what elevates the spirit.

For it seems to me that all things which exist—every creature, every phenomenon, every flowing form—derive their purpose and their being from the divine source that authored creation itself. In this truth lies a profound lesson: even the humblest of existing things can instruct us in matters of duty and rightful conduct, if only we possess the wisdom to perceive it. It is this pursuit of understanding, this desire to extract wisdom from all that surrounds me, that compels my contemplation.

Yet I recognize that such communion with the divine is not granted freely to every disposition. Only a soul that remains healthy and undefiled can hope to establish this sacred connection. Whatever has become infected by corruption, whatever has descended into depravity, whatever lies spiritually lifeless—these conditions render a person incapable of sympathy with the divine nature. The doorway to higher truth remains closed to hearts that harbor such afflictions, for like cannot commune with unlike, and purity cannot mingle with decay.

What is required, instead, is a restless and unceasing desire—a longing for divine light and for that vital, animating fire which sustains all true understanding. This yearning functions as an irresistible force within the soul, drawing and guiding the seeker much as physical beauty commands and captivates the eye. This is no ordinary desire that might be quenched by circumstance or twisted aside by distraction; it burns with a persistence that outlasts every obstacle placed before it.

When this pure and celestial longing takes firm root within a person, and continues to grow without ever tiring or diminishing, something remarkable occurs: God Himself establishes a sacred communion with that soul. Hidden truths are revealed, mysteries once concealed become illuminated, and profound blessing descends upon those who offer their heart to this pursuit fully, without hesitation or reluctance. It is through this complete and willing surrender that the seeker finds themselves drawn ever closer to the very source of wisdom and truth they have sought all along.

# On the Nature of Longing

*A Meditation*

There is a stream I have watched by moonlight, silver and unceasing, that moves without instruction toward some destination it cannot name yet never doubts. I have sat upon its bank for hours, wondering at the mystery of its motion—not the mechanics that scholars might explain, but the deeper riddle: why does it move at all? What draws it onward with such quiet certainty?

The water does not pause to question its course. It does not deliberate whether the sea exists, or whether the journey is worthwhile. It simply flows, obedient to something written into its very substance, a restless, pure desire that predates thought and survives all obstacle. Boulders divert it; still it finds a way. Drought diminishes it; still it seeks the lower ground, the gathering place, the vast water that calls all rivers home.

I have come to believe this movement is no mere accident of physics, but a parable written in liquid light. For does not the same law govern the deepest chambers of the human heart? We too are called toward a Source we cannot fully comprehend, and something in us—when we are most truly ourselves—longs for that higher radiance the way water longs for the sea, the way growing things lean toward the sun without being taught to do so.

The moonlight upon the water does not create the stream's movement; it merely reveals what was already occurring in the dark. So too does grace not manufacture our longing for God—it illuminates a yearning that was always present, however buried beneath the sediment of distraction and doubt. The pure desire was there before we noticed it shimmering.

Consider the herbs that grow in hidden places—in forest shadow, in mountain cleft, unseen by any human eye, uncelebrated by any hand. No one waters them. No one prunes or protects them. Yet they thrive, because something deeper than human attention sustains them: sunlight finding its way through leaves, rain finding its way through soil, roots finding their way toward what nourishes. Their flourishing is quiet, unwitnessed, but no less real for being hidden.

So it is, I think, with genuine devotion. The soul that turns toward the divine with unyielding desire—not desire performed for others to see, not devotion measured in visible achievement, but the restless, pure longing that moves like water toward its source—that soul discovers within this very desire a sacred connection already forming, already deepening, whether or not the world takes notice.

This is the promise embedded in nature's patient teaching: what moves toward its true home cannot fail to arrive. What seeks the light, however slowly, however invisibly, will find the light seeking it in return. The water reaches the sea. The herb finds its nourishment. And the heart that longs, wholly and without pretense, for God, becomes—in that very longing—already joined to what it seeks.

This is not passivity but the deepest activity: the arrow's flight toward what has already claimed it, before it ever leaves the bow. The renewal is not earned through display, nor rewarded for being witnessed, but assured simply because desire, when pure and unbroken, participates already in the reality it seeks. Truth reveals itself not to the loudest seeker, but to the one who moves, like water in moonlight, toward the source that made the longing possible in the first place.
outputs.L5:
# Whatever You Focus On, Attracts More of the Same

There's an old idea, found in various forms across philosophy, psychology, and spiritual traditions, that suggests our attention shapes our reality more than we realize. Whatever occupies our thoughts most consistently tends to expand its presence in our lives—and this isn't necessarily mystical, but observable in very practical ways.

Consider someone who constantly worries about scarcity. Their mind, tuned to lack, notices every sign of it: the rising prices, the missed opportunities, the things they don't have. Meanwhile, someone focused on abundance notices different things—the resources available, the possibilities emerging, the connections forming. Same world, different lens, different reality experienced.

This isn't about ignoring problems or pretending difficulties don't exist. Whatever challenges we face are real, and acknowledging them matters. But there's a difference between acknowledging a problem and *dwelling* in it. The dwelling is where the attraction happens—not in some magical sense, but through:

**Selective attention** — We notice what confirms our existing focus, filtering out contradictory information almost unconsciously.

**Behavioral alignment** — Our actions naturally shift to match our dominant thoughts. Fear breeds cautious, defensive behavior. Confidence breeds bold, exploratory behavior. And these behaviors create different outcomes.

**Emotional contagion** — People and opportunities respond to our energy. Whatever mood we project tends to attract corresponding responses from others.

The practical takeaway isn't "think positive and everything works out"—that's an oversimplification that ignores real-world complexity. Instead, it's an invitation to notice: What am I habitually focusing on? And is that focus serving the life I actually want to build?

Sometimes whatever attracts our attention isn't something we chose consciously—old fears, inherited beliefs, cultural conditioning. Becoming aware of these patterns is the first step toward choosing more deliberately what deserves our focus, and consequently, what we allow to grow in our experience.

In the end, the relationship between attention and attraction isn't a guarantee of outcomes, but a reminder of agency: we have more influence over our inner focus than we often exercise, and that focus—whatever it may be—shapes the reality we inhabit.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a metaphysical poem in the style of Henry Vaughan about a flower or plant that longs for sunlight, using it as an allegory for the soul's desire for God.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Heliotrope**

I saw a flower, low and dim,
That all day turned to follow Him—
The sun, whose face she never held,
Yet by whose light she lived, and swelled

Her secret cup toward that far fire,
As if mere looking were desire
Enough to bridge the gulf of miles
Between her root and heaven's smiles.

O soul, thou art this tender thing,
Rooted in dust, yet quickening
Toward some undying, distant blaze
Thou canst not touch, but only gaze!

We call this world our home, and yet
We turn like her, with eyes still wet,
Toward that first Light we half recall—
Before the fall, before the Fall,

When every leaf and living breath
Knew nothing yet of night or death,
But stood, plain vessels, brimmed with day,
No shadow yet to cross their way.

Now clouds oft hide the Sun we seek,
And still we turn, though bruised and weak,
For something deep within the seed
Remembers Light, and turns, and pleads.

Poor flower! thy patient, silent art
Is but the pattern of my heart:
To lean all day toward what I lack,
And trust the dark will send Him back—

That He who set thee first to grow
Beneath His warmth, His overflow,
Will not forget the thing He made,
Nor leave thee lost in permanent shade,

But when this vein of clay is dry,
And all my leaves turned pale to die,
Will draw me up past root and rain
Into that Light which knows no wane.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a 17th-century-style devotional poem addressing "thee" (some natural object like a heliotrope or sunflower) that turns toward light, exploring themes of divine communion and pure desire.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon the Heliotrope, Turning to the Sun**
*A Meditation*

Thou humble vassal of the light,
That know'st no worship but the true,
Whose golden face, from morn till night,
Doth still the glorious sun pursue;

No forc'd obedience bends thy stem,
No feign'd allegiance moves thy eye,
But love, love only, guides the gem
Of thy small world unto the sky.

O that my soul might learn of thee
This constancy, this pure desire!
For thou dost teach philosophy
Beyond what learn'd schools require:

That to be plant, and yet to know
The path of light, and still pursue,
Is more than man, who feels the glow
Of grace, yet turns his face from view.

Thou canst not choose but follow him
Who feeds thee with his daily beam;
I, having choice, do choose the dim
And treach'rous shadows of a dream.

Teach me, thou silent priest of day,
To fix mine eye as thine is fix'd;
Not to be dazzled, nor to stray,
Nor have my love with error mix'd.

So when the Sun of Righteousness
*(Mal. iv. 2)*
Shall rise with healing in his wings,
My soul, though small, may thee confess
Her pattern, and thus learn to sing:

"I have no light but what is giv'n,
No motion but tow'rd my day;
Thou art my sun, O Christ, my heav'n,
And I thy heliotrope alway."
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem imitating the metaphysical poets (like Vaughan or Herbert) that uses the image of a plant seeking the sun to symbolize the soul seeking God, ending with a note on grace and renewal?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Heliotrope's Devotion

Not by my own contrivance do I turn,
But some deep pull, some ancient debt I owe
To light I did not make, yet daily burn
To find, as if I'd known it long ago.

See how the stem, that green and humble thread,
Twists all day long to keep the sun in view—
No eye to see, no mind to be misled,
Yet still it knows the one thing it must do.

So does my soul, though blinder far than this,
Grope through the tangled dark for Thee, my Sun,
Not knowing half the time what it should miss,
Nor how such crooked seeking could be won.

I am no help to my own turning, Lord—
The plant at least obeys a natural law;
But I resist the pull, distrust the cord,
And call each shadow's comfort what I saw.

Yet Thou, who set the flower's face aright,
Who tuned its cells to seek what they cannot known,
Dost stoop to bend my darker, stubborn night
Until it learns to lean where it is shown.

What grace is this, that waits on such as me—
That does not wait for merit to begin,
But finds the seed still folded in its plea
And coaxes bloom from what was cold within?

Each morning, look: the flower does not doubt
The sun will rise, though night has been so long.
So teach my heart this turning, self-cast-out,
Till facing Thee becomes my only song.

And when I fail—as fail I will, and must—
Let not the turning cease, though I grow dim;
For grace regreens the stem bowed low in dust,
And every dawn begins my life in Him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a religious/metaphysical poem with archaic diction ("thee," "thou," "imbars") reflecting on how a natural phenomenon's constant turning toward light teaches humans about spiritual longing and divine commerce.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Heliotrope's Homily

Thou turnest, humble flower, toward the sun,
As I would turn my soul when day is done—
Not by command of root or stem alone,
But by some deeper hunger, yet unknown,
That pulls thy face where light doth first appear
And keeps thee faithful through the darkened year.

What holy geometry imbars thy bloom
Within this endless, patient, golden room?
Thou hast no eyes to see, no mind to know,
Yet thou dost seek the light where'er it go—
A pilgrim rooted, yet no less a guide
To those whose hearts in shadow long abide.

O let me learn thy silent liturgy:
To bend, to turn, to face what I cannot see
Directly, but must trust as thou dost trust
That light returns each morning from the dust
Of yesternight's despair. Thou dost not ask
Why darkness comes, but keep thy patient task—

Thy commerce with the sun a sacrament,
Exchanging shadow for thy nourishment,
As I would trade my doubt, my wandering will,
For that same light which doth thy petals fill.
Teach me, thou humble priest of field and stone,
How constancy makes prayer of flesh and bone.

For if a flower, mute and rooted fast,
Can hold such faithful vigil to the last—
Can turn and turn again through storm and grief
Toward light it cannot touch, past all belief—
Then how much more should I, who thinking, breathe,
Turn toward the Light that all my longing wreathe?

Thou askest nothing but to greet the dawn;
I ask for meaning when the light is drawn
Away from me in trials, dark and long—
Yet thou dost teach: this turning is the song.
Not answer, but the asking is the prayer;
Not arrival, but the turning there.

So let my spirit, like thy golden face,
Imbar itself within that sacred space
Between the seeking and the sought-for light,
Between the doubting and the burning bright—
For thou hast shown, O humble, faithful bloom,
That longing is the light within the room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in rhymed couplets, echoing 17th-century religious verse, personifying a heliotrope or similar plant and drawing a moral lesson about desire, purity, and God's grace from its behavior.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Heliotrope**

Behold this humble flower, small and slight,
That turns her face forever toward the light;
No storm can shake her purpose, nor deter
The constant faith that God has planted her.
When morning breaks upon her dewy head,
She lifts herself as one but newly wed
To that great Sun whose rays she cannot own,
Yet seeks Him only, for Him alone.

O foolish heart of man, that strays and roams
Through worldly gardens, seeking other homes
For its affection, when one Light doth shine
That asks but this—that we like her incline!
The flower knows no cunning, no deceit,
She does not calculate what path is meet,
But by an instinct deeper than her root
She turns, she yearns, she bears the Sun for fruit.

How like our souls, which Grace alone can bend
Toward that first Love which knows nor change nor end!
For we, corrupted by our own desire,
Do turn toward earthly and consuming fire—
Toward gold, toward flesh, toward vanity and pride—
While she, more wise, has never turned aside.
Her purity is this: she wants but one,
And gives her whole self to the rising sun.

Teach me, small teacher, lesson though it be
From lowly stem and leaf, humility—
That my desires, so scattered and so wild,
Might learn the fixed devotion of a child
Who knows but one true Father, and no other,
Who needs no idol, mistress, gold, nor mother
To fill the aching hollow of the breast,
But turns to Christ, and there alone finds rest.

For as she cannot help but seek the light,
Nor turn her petals to the falling night,
So let my will, once crooked, now be bent
Not by my strength, but by Thy grace's dint,
Until, transformed like her, I too shall be
A creature wholly turned, my God, to Thee—
Not for the beauty that the world can give,
But for that Light in whom alone I live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
